issues.legal_issue: A revisional court may not reweigh evidence on a factual issue affecting jurisdiction when the subordinate court’s finding is supported by the record.
material_facts: The subordinate court found that the summons had not been served and that the application to set aside the ex parte decree was not time-barred.
The High Court, exercising revisional jurisdiction, reassessed the evidence about service and the applicant’s knowledge and substituted its own factual conclusions.
The Supreme Court found that the subordinate court’s findings were supported by the evidence and that the High Court’s contrary inference rested on conjecture.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded the limits of revisional jurisdiction by reassessing the evidence and substituting its findings for those of the subordinate court.
issues.legal_principle: Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure confines revision to jurisdictional errors. Although a limitation issue may require deciding a collateral question of fact affecting jurisdiction, a revisional court cannot reassess evidence and substitute its findings unless the subordinate court’s finding is unsupported by the evidence, manifestly contrary to it, or palpably wrong such that grave injustice would result.

predicates.revision_proceeding: A higher court is reviewing a subordinate court’s decision in revision rather than hearing a first appeal.
predicates.jurisdictional_collateral_fact: The subordinate court’s jurisdiction depends on a factual issue, such as whether a proceeding is barred by limitation.
predicates.supported_factual_finding: The subordinate court’s finding on that factual issue is supported by the evidence and is not manifestly contrary to the record or palpably wrong.

issues.definition: When a revision concerns a jurisdictional factual issue and the subordinate court’s finding is supported by the evidence, the revisional court cannot substitute its own assessment of that evidence.

issues.legal_issue: When summons was not duly served, the limitation period for an application to set aside an ex parte decree runs from the applicant’s knowledge of the decree.
material_facts: The applicant applied to set aside the ex parte decree after learning of it from a relative in the first week of November 1975.
The application was filed on December 2, 1975.
The suit record showed no direction for issuing summons to the applicant, and the process server’s return and testimony were found unreliable.
The applicant’s account that he had not been served and had learned of the decree only shortly before applying was not rebutted by testimony from the opposing parties.
issues.conclusion: The application was not barred by limitation, and the order setting aside the ex parte decree was confirmed as against the applicant.
issues.legal_principle: Article 123 of the Limitation Act, 1963, provides a thirty-day period to apply to set aside an ex parte decree, running from the decree when summons was duly served and from knowledge of the decree when summons was not duly served. Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure provides for setting aside an ex parte decree in the relevant circumstances. Order V Rules 19 and 19A and the pre-amendment Order IX Rule 6(1) govern inquiry into service and proceeding ex parte. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.application_to_set_aside_ex_parte_decree: A party applies to set aside a decree made in that party’s absence.
predicates.summons_not_duly_served: The party was not duly served with summons in the proceeding that resulted in the decree.
predicates.filed_within_limitation_from_knowledge: The application was filed within the applicable limitation period measured from the party’s knowledge of the decree.

issues.definition: An application to set aside an ex parte decree is not time-barred when summons was not duly served and the application was filed within the limitation period measured from the applicant’s knowledge of the decree.

issues.legal_issue: Relief setting aside an ex parte decree may be confined to the applicant when another affected defendant has not challenged the decree and the opposing party agrees that the decree need not otherwise be disturbed.
material_facts: The compromise decree allocated all the suit properties among parties who had compromised, including awarding the business property to one of them.
The appeal concerned the applicant’s claimed interest in that business property.
Another defendant affected by the ex parte decree had not sought to set it aside and did not appear in the appeal.
Counsel for the opposing parties stated that the party receiving the business property would not seek compensation from the other properties if the applicant established his interest.
issues.conclusion: The decree was set aside only as against the applicant; the suit as against him was to proceed on the basis that the compromise was not binding on him.
issues.legal_principle: In determining the extent of relief, the Court considered that the applicant alone pursued the challenge, the other defendant had accepted the decree, and counsel for the opposing parties stated that the decree need not be disturbed as to the remaining property allocation if the applicant succeeded in establishing his interest. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.appeal_from_ex_parte_decree: A party appeals from a decision concerning an ex parte decree.
predicates.applicant_succeeds_in_challenge: The applicant establishes grounds for setting aside the decree as against that applicant.
predicates.other_affected_defendant_does_not_challe: Another affected defendant does not pursue a challenge to the decree.
predicates.opposing_party_disclaims_compensation_cl: The opposing party states that it will not seek compensation from other property if the applicant establishes the claimed interest.

issues.definition: When an applicant succeeds in challenging an ex parte decree, another affected defendant does not challenge it, and the opposing party disclaims a compensation claim against other property, the decree is set aside only as to the applicant.
